decision: probed the machine for toolchain and model credentials before planning anything
why: did not want to design against assumptions about what was installed
evidence: powershell probe of node/npm/bun/git/gh/python and env vars
result: no node on PATH, no LLM key of any kind, git and gh and python present

decision: tested the gh token against GitHub Models instead of assuming it would work
why: whether a credential works is measurable, so measuring beat guessing
evidence: live call to models.github.ai catalog and inference endpoints
result: both returned HTTP 410, GitHub Models was retired 2026-07-30, path permanently closed

decision: found node was already installed rather than missing
why: winget said the package existed, so the real problem was a stale PATH not a missing install
evidence: winget list OpenJS.NodeJS.LTS, node --version after prepending the dir
result: node 24.19.0 and npm 11.17.0 work, every node command must prepend the winget portable dir

decision: treated the dev box and the production host as different hardware
why: dev here has no GPU at all, production is a 4090 with 24GB, so a GPU-dependent test suite would be unrunnable locally
evidence: Win32_VideoController shows only Hyper-V Video, nvidia-smi absent
result: engine tests must run against a deterministic fake DM, real model smoke-tested separately

decision: made a bootstrap commit on main so feature worktrees could exist
why: a brand new repo has no HEAD, and worktrees need one
result: main has a root commit, .worktrees/ is gitignored

decision: created the feature worktree and did all work there
why: house rule is that the primary checkout is never edited directly
result: worktree live, primary root resolves correctly from inside it

decision: built a model probe before designing the DM contract
why: the contract depends on whether a local model can be trusted to emit valid actions, and that is a number not an opinion
result: probe runs three decoding modes and validates against real engine invariants

decision: measured three decoding modes against a real local model
why: wanted the comparison against a baseline rather than just testing the mode I expected to win
evidence: probe output, 8 trials each on qwen2.5:3b-instruct
result: unconstrained 0/8, plain JSON mode 0/8, schema-constrained 8/8

decision: rejected plain JSON mode despite it parsing on every trial
why: it parsed 8/8 and was still wrong 8/8, emitting capital-N Narration and no intent at all
result: a parse-only gate would have scored it perfect, so the gate had to check shape not syntax

decision: split model failure into two classes and only claimed one was solved
why: constrained decoding fixes shape, it cannot stop a schema-valid action from being rules-illegal
result: engine still owns rules validation, that is now the only place model output can be rejected

decision: dropped the transpiler and test framework from the plan
why: node 24 runs .ts directly and node --test handles .ts, so ts-node and jest and vitest all earn nothing
evidence: ran a .ts file and a .ts test directly, both passed
result: API tier and engine tests need zero build tooling

decision: sent the DM contract to four competing designs instead of picking one
why: it is a one-way door, and a wrong call here means either a DM that hallucinates HP or a DM that cannot improvise
evidence: four background runners on claude-opus-5, gpt-5.6-sol, grok-4.5, gemini-3.8-flash
result: open

decision: pushed the probe result to the running candidates mid-flight
why: they were designing a parse-repair ladder for a problem the runtime already eliminates
result: all four acknowledged, still running

decision: took candidate 1 as the synthesis base
why: it was the only one that made illegal actions undecodable instead of merely rejected, by building the JSON schema per turn from live world state
result: open

decision: measured candidate 1's own open question instead of leaving it open
why: it flagged that long target enums might degrade choice quality, and that is measurable so it was not the operator's to answer
result: confirmed the risk is real and worse than expected

decision: found that enum validity stays perfect while enum correctness collapses
why: at 25 entities the model still always picked a valid target and picked the RIGHT one only 3 of 8 times, usually attacking an unarmed old woman
result: in-enum 24/24 across all sizes, correct 8/8 then 4/8 then 3/8

decision: made inReach scoping a load-bearing rule rather than a convenience
why: a generous target list is actively harmful and no validity metric would ever report it
evidence: brief.ts scopeCast in the synthesized design
result: open, needs a cap and a test enforcing it

decision: left the project uncatalogued at the operator's request
why: asked because it is a preference no experiment settles, and the answer was skip
result: worktree and branching rules still followed this session, nothing persists to the next

decision: synthesized the four candidates into one design package
why: candidate 1 was the base, with named grafts from the other three and re-prompting rejected outright
result: tsc --noEmit exits 0, verified independently not taken on trust

decision: cut the mint slots from 4 to 2 after the merge caught a hole in my own instruction
why: capping inReach at 6 still gave a decoder enum of 10 once mint slots were added, which is exactly the 4-of-8 condition I was trying to avoid
evidence: director.ts MAX_TARGET_ENUM derived from MAX_IN_REACH plus MINT_SLOTS
result: total enum bounded at 8 and derived rather than duplicated

decision: accepted the worker's refusal to force three outcomes into one union
why: rewrite and drop are per-effect and co-occur, soft-fail is a property of the whole turn, so one union would have had to lie
evidence: AdmissionReport and TurnResult in the package
result: my instruction was wrong and was corrected rather than worked around

decision: installed ollama and pulled a small model on the GPU-less box
why: every measurement in this trail depends on it, and the trail did not record where the numbers came from
result: serving on 11434, added retroactively during the self-audit

decision: my own audit grep reported a missing hostileDirector that was present all along
why: the pattern matched export const and export function but not export declare const, so the check was wrong not the delegate
result: false negative, logged because the same class of error is what this run kept hunting

decision: ran the mandatory cross-model review of this trail on a different model family
why: the work was done by claude-opus-5 so self-review could not catch its own blind spots
result: three checked findings all confirmed true

decision: SUPERSEDES the enum-degradation rows. the length effect does not exist
why: the reviewer found the conditions used different distractors. the attractor sat at index 5 so it was absent from the 3-entity case and present in the larger ones, which manufactured the trend
result: corrected run 6/8 3/8 3/8 4/8 6/8 for sizes 3 6 8 10 25, no trend

decision: MAX_IN_REACH 6 now has no evidence behind it and must be revisited
why: it was derived by interpolating a trend that turned out to be an artifact of my own experiment design
result: open, the cap is unjustified not necessarily wrong

decision: gave the unconstrained and json-mode baselines the field names they were never shown
why: the original comparison only told schema mode what shape to produce, so a baseline failure could have meant cannot comply or was never asked
result: not yet re-run, the fair-baseline number is still unknown

decision: closed the transport gap the reviewer flagged as most dangerous
why: both probes measured /api/generate while the design advertises /v1, so the guarantee might not have transferred
result: /v1 with response_format json_schema also 8/8, gap closed favourably

decision: built the runnable slice instead of generating a verification skill against unimplemented bodies
why: the create-verification-skill skill says to fix a non-running base first, and every body was still not implemented
result: 17 tests green with no GPU, tsc clean

decision: mutation tested every engine rule against only its own named test
why: a mutant killed by the full suite does not show the test named for the rule is the one that caught it
result: 7/7 killed, each by its own named test

decision: found a real bug by looking at a screenshot that every green check had missed
why: the player's own words never reached the transcript, because the client rendered them optimistically then replaced them with a server view that never stored them
result: fixed by putting the utterance in the event log, two regression tests added

decision: generated and then actually executed the verification skill
why: an unexecuted skill is a draft, so the take-a-turn recipe was run exactly as written
result: 6/6 assertions PASS, evidence survived cleanup

decision: SUPERSEDES the evidence paths in the two rows above. they point at evidence/ which was later moved
why: commit 9243244 relocated the kept artifacts and gitignored the scratch directory, which broke the pointers
result: paths corrected here rather than by editing history

decision: second cross-model review found the central claim was false in the shipped code
why: rulings were collected in a local array and turned into events by a trailing loop that three early returns jumped straight over
result: every dropped intent was ruled on and then silently discarded

decision: emitted rulings at the decision point instead of in a trailing loop
why: fixing the three early returns would have left the next early return free to reintroduce it, so the shape was the bug
result: drops and failed-roll rewrites now reach the log, two mutants prove it

decision: gave adjudicate a working world that absorbs its own events
why: a freshly minted NPC was only in the events array, so a lookup against the stale world returned undefined and it could never die
result: an NPC invented this turn can now be killed this turn

decision: added an engage op, because combat was unreachable
why: attack is undecodable during exploration by design and nothing anywhere transitioned into combat, so the game could never leave peace
result: combat is now reachable and still exits when the last foe falls

decision: derived minted ids from the world seed and event count
why: the old id used a module counter reset by restart and a timestamp that wraps every 28 minutes, so two sessions could collide and replay was not deterministic
result: same world mints the same id, different seeds do not collide

decision: expanded the mutation harness from 7 rules to 17
why: the reviewer pointed out that 7 of 7 sounded complete while damage capping, absent targets and combat exit had no mutant at all
result: the expanded run immediately exposed 3 stale anchors and 2 genuinely uncovered rules

decision: wrote the two tests the surviving mutants demanded
why: removing engage from the schema and removing the absent-target drop both left their tests passing, which means those rules were not covered
result: 17/17 mutants now killed by their own named test

decision: read the operator's real 10-turn session out of the event log
why: they asked whether the log could drive improvements, and it is far better evidence than any scenario I invented
evidence: data/portale.db, copied read-only so the live session was untouched
result: 10 turns produced zero rolls, zero damage, zero rulings

decision: found the log could not answer why
why: the design called refusals telemetry and then never recorded which op the DM chose, so the most important question was unanswerable
result: added a proposed event, never shown to the player

decision: built a replay probe over the real transcript instead of inventing test scenes
why: the defects only appeared in real play, so the real play is the test corpus
result: baseline reproduced it exactly, narrate_only 10 of 10 and combat intent 0 of 4

decision: moved op ahead of narration in the schema
why: constrained decoding emits fields in declaration order, so the model wrote hundreds of words of prose and then picked an op to match what it had already written
result: the narrate_only monoculture ended immediately

decision: gave out-of-character messages an op enum with one member
why: asking the model nicely did not work. the player typed I just told you I stabbed him in the eye, keep up, and was attacked for it, because the sentence is full of violence
result: starting a fight over a meta comment went from 2 of 2 to 0 of 2, and is now undecodable

decision: chose over-eager combat over dropped attacks when tempering engage
why: tempering to stop false positives reintroduced a dropped stabbing. an early fight can be talked down, an erased action is the original complaint
result: violence dropped back to 0 of 4 across two consecutive runs

decision: my own out-of-character heuristic was disarming a real action
why: the keep up pattern matched I tell the dockhand to keep up as we run, which would have silently cancelled a legitimate turn
result: pattern removed, the real utterance still matches on ending with DM

decision: the minted-id test was passing on timing rather than on the property
why: it compared two ids, and a clock-based id also compares equal inside one millisecond and unequal across a tick, so it survived a Date.now mutant
result: rewritten to assert the id begins with the world seed, mutant now dies

decision: made engage resolve the blow that started the fight
why: driving the live model showed it entering combat and then discarding the stab, so the DM narrated a wound the world never took. that is the original bug wearing a different hat
evidence: rules.ts engage falls through to resolution
result: a roll and damage now happen on the turn combat begins

decision: told the DM to narrate the attempt and never the result
why: it wrote the dagger piercing her eye on a turn the roll then failed, so the prose and the die openly contradicted each other
evidence: director.ts narration rules with a wrong and right example
result: decided-the-outcome went from routine to 1 of 10

decision: raised the repetition penalties after the narration fix made repetition worse
why: a narrower brief leaves fewer ways to open a sentence, so constraining the prose pushed repeats from 1 of 10 to 5 of 10
result: back to 1 of 10, and op quality rose to 9 of 10 at the same time

decision: checked the dice before fixing them, and there was nothing to fix
why: three critical misses in a row looked like a broken generator, but 40000 rolls came out uniform at min 1904 max 2099
result: the repeats were my display window plus seq 2 and seq 6 both mapping to face 1 under seed 777

decision: scrubbed bookkeeping tokens out of narration at the boundary
why: the live DM opened a narration with ~new3 introduces, naming a slot that does not exist. asking it not to is necessary and not sufficient
result: the engine now replaces ids with names and slot tokens with someone

decision: my first scrub only covered the two declared slots and let the invented one through
why: the model wrote ~new3 and MINT_SLOTS only lists ~new1 and ~new2, so the test I had just written failed on the real input
evidence: rules.ts regex over any slot-shaped token
result: 34 tests, 23 of 23 mutants

decision: found the HTTP layer had no tests at all
why: unit tests never touch HTTP and the browser harness goes through the UI, so routing, status codes, the in-flight guard and traversal were unverified
result: 21 API tests added

decision: split the server into a constructible app and a thin entry
why: it built everything at module scope and listened on import, so nothing could test it in process
result: tests now build a real server on an ephemeral port with a scripted DM

decision: added a typed client and a CLI so the API can be driven without a browser
why: the operator asked for a direct line to the server, and a raw escape hatch is what makes status codes assertable
result: smoke passes 10 checks and exits non-zero on failure

decision: two of my own new API tests were passing for the wrong reason
why: the traversal test used a path with no file behind it so it 404d either way, and the body-limit test sent an oversized utterance that the length check caught first
result: fixed with a real canary file and short-utterance padding, 30 of 30 mutants now die

decision: fixed a libuv assertion on shutdown
why: closing the database inside the server close callback tore down a handle that was still closing
result: CLI now exits cleanly with the right code

decision: the live pass caught drift I had just written into the map
why: I added an out-of-character recipe that cannot work under the scripted DM, because that director never reads the schema the guard collapses
result: marked live-model-only and re-proved against the real model, no new roll added

decision: researched what players hate about AI dungeon masters
why: the operator asked me to incorporate DM craft, and the literature is blunt about the top failure
result: yes-manning. the world never pushes back and choices carry no consequence

decision: found the game had that failure in its purest form
why: the protagonist appeared in the rules only as the roller, never as a target, so you could stab the same smuggler forever and take nothing back
result: no opposition existed at all

decision: gave the engine the reprisal, not the model
why: a world that only fights back when the narrator remembers to is not a world. the engine picks the foe and rolls; the DM is merely told so it can narrate the blow coming
result: player hp now falls, and the player can lose

decision: routed every exit from adjudicate through one finish() function
why: reprisals placed after the early returns would have been the rulings bug a second time, stranded behind the same six returns
result: two mutants prove a reprisal survives both a missed swing and a dropped intent

decision: my fallen-player test was passing on a missed counterblow
why: it asserted no damage reached a downed player, but the seed produced no counterblow at all, so the guard was never exercised
result: rewritten to search for a seed where the blow lands first, 36 of 36 mutants now die

decision: checked the dice again before believing a repeat
why: two reprisals rolled 6 in a row, which looked like a stuck generator
evidence: 4000 consecutive seq for seed 606, min 175 max 228
result: uniform. seq indices 9 and 15 both map to 6, so it was coincidence

decision: gave the world geography, because the map feature had nowhere to live
why: one room, no movement, nothing to explore. a map of a single room is not a map
result: the Drowned Lantern now has a common room, cellar, yard and dock

decision: built the direction enum from the current room's real exits
why: the same trick the rest of the contract uses. the DM cannot walk you through a wall because a wall is not in the enum
result: a bad direction is undecodable, and a stale one is refused

decision: scoped reach and reprisals to the room the player is standing in
why: without it a foe keeps swinging from the room you left, and the DM can name someone two rooms away
result: two mutants cover both halves

decision: deleted the introduce op rather than adding another rule about it
why: the DM reached for it constantly and then left introduces null, earning a refusal. minting is keyed on the target being a slot, so the op bought nothing
result: removing the choice removed the failure

decision: best replay score of the project after that deletion
why: subtraction beat every prompt rule I have written for this model
result: op defensible 9 of 10, and truncated, repeated, leaked, menu and outcome-deciding all zero

decision: named a condition so the mutation harness could target it
why: the bare combat check appears three times in rules.ts, so a string replace would silently mutate the reprisal instead of the movement guard
result: the rule is now individually killable

decision: research ranked progress clocks as the cheapest high-impact thing left
why: the game had opposition but nothing accumulated, so no turn mattered more than any other
evidence: gpt-5.6-sol research, Blades in the Dark progress clocks
result: clocks are engine-owned pressure the player can see

decision: the DM nominates a clock, the engine decides the step
why: same division as everywhere else. the enum holds only clocks already in play, so the model can apply pressure but cannot invent it or resolve a threat early
result: a clock the DM invented is refused with a ruling

decision: caught a projection bug while writing it, before it shipped
why: the transcript read filled off the final world, so every historical tick would have rendered today's number
result: a test now asserts the ticks read 1/6 2/6 3/6 rather than 3/6 three times

decision: a surviving mutant told me a condition was dead code
why: removing !after.done changed nothing, because the earlier target.done guard already returned, so the check could never fire
result: split the guard in two so each half is individually killable, and deleted the redundancy

decision: gave the player a vow, because the session still had no point
why: research put an Ironsworn vow second only to clocks. without one a session is unrelated turns, which is the difference between a game and a conversation with dice
result: ten boxes on screen from the first turn

decision: the engine refuses a milestone the turn did not earn
why: the DM may claim ground, but a claim needs a successful roll, a wound, a death, a filled clock or a move behind it. otherwise a narrator can talk the player to their goal
result: unearned-milestone is a ruling the player reads

decision: used the proposal telemetry to diagnose a wasted turn, rather than guessing
why: a live session showed op=skill_check target=~new1, so the op was right and the target was wrong, and the whole turn was being thrown away
evidence: proposed event in the session log
result: this is the first time that telemetry paid for itself

decision: only violence requires a valid target now
why: a skill check is an attempt against a difficulty, not against a person, so a fumbled target should not cost the player their turn
result: the check is rolled, the turn is not wasted

decision: the harness found dead code twice in one feature
why: removing a condition changed nothing both times, because an earlier guard had already returned
evidence: rules.ts applyTick and the target guard
result: both deleted, 56 of 56 mutants now die

decision: best replay score of the project, a perfect op score
why: every structural change so far has moved this number, and prompt rules mostly have not
result: op defensible 10 of 10, all fatal metrics zero, one repeat

decision: caught myself editing README in the primary checkout and moved it to a worktree
why: house rule is that the primary checkout is never edited, and I broke it
result: change relocated, primary left clean

decision: built the map generator graph-first rather than geometry-first
why: research was blunt that topology decides whether a dungeon is worth exploring, not floorplan. a spanning tree is a corridor you walk down and back
result: Jaquays loop pass costs one extra step

decision: a property test caught the generator producing pure corridors
why: seven example seeds passed while 38 of 400 were trees. a generator needs a sample wide enough to hit the rare shape
result: fixed by compact growth plus a guaranteed bridge, 0 of 5000 now

decision: added a brief-reading DM because the scripted one is welded to the tavern
why: pointed at a generated delve it named a smuggler who was not there, and the engine correctly refused every turn, so generated content could not be exercised at all
result: PORTALE_DM=wander walks any scenario with no model

decision: strengthened a test that passed for the wrong reason
why: it asserted nothing was refused, which stays true when the DM simply never fights, so the mutation survived
result: now asserts a hostile in the room is engaged, 62 of 62 mutants die

decision: drove the two new feature files live before shipping them
why: a feature map written from source alone documents the app you believe you built. the live pass disproved two of my own preconditions
result: 21 asserts pass, two recipes corrected before merge

decision: found that a fresh session is not a fresh script
why: both deterministic DMs hold their cursor in the director, which server.ts builds once per process, so session two starts mid-script and never sees the opening engage
result: take-a-turn and engine-authority preconditions corrected to require a fresh server

decision: stopped the engine ruling on a field the op never reads
why: every walk into an empty room printed 'the DM reached for a new character'. the schema forces target to be filled, so on a move it is noise, and crying wolf costs the one mechanism that makes engine authority visible
result: spurious ruling gone in the browser, rulings still fire for violence, 64 of 64 mutants die

decision: retracted my own claim that the replay probe measured the fix
why: i argued the probe's 9 of 10 could be causal because rulings feed back into the prompt. it cannot: the probe never imports rules.ts and never calls adjudicate, so the drop is sampling noise at temp 0.85
evidence: replay-probe/run.mjs imports director, engine, world, dice only
result: probe scores the model in isolation, not the played game. worth knowing before trusting it

decision: deleted packages/engine and rewrote the module map against real exports
why: 1851 lines of orphaned TypeScript that nothing imported, while docs/design/module-map.md described it as THE architecture. a reader following the docs studied dead code
evidence: no value or type import from packages/app, 106 tests and tsc unchanged after deletion
result: map now documents the 11 live modules, and verifying the dependency graph exposed a type-only cycle between engine and mapgen that my own diagram had hidden

decision: clues, and a vow that only advances on discovery
why: vows advanced on any earned turn, so winning a fight moved an investigation forward. that is yes-manning wearing a progress bar
evidence: rules.ts stillHidden gate, world.ts Clue, 4 clues in the lantern and 3 per delve
result: 114 tests, 70 of 70 mutants, both paths driven in a real browser

decision: re-ran the enum probe properly at 30 trials and confirmed the retraction
why: the cap MAX_IN_REACH=8 was justified by a finding withdrawn in september. correctness by enum size is 15, 11, 13, 8, 15 out of 30 for sizes 3, 6, 8, 10, 25. no trend
result: list length does not drive correctness. one attractor causes 17 of 22 errors at size 10, and it is not an enum-position artefact

decision: the enum attractor experiment: removing one distractor doubled correctness at size 8
why: 13 of 30 became 27 of 30 with the knitting old woman deleted. at size 25 the same deletion changed nothing, 15 became 13, because a hooded scribe took over as the attractor
result: the model reaches for the most salient person, not the named one. length matters only because long lists are likelier to hold a strong attractor

decision: ranked the entity the player named to the front of inReach
why: writing the doc exposed that the code sorted on hostility alone, so the claim that the named person never falls off the cap was aspirational
result: the crowded-room test first passed without the fix on insertion order; fillers had to be made hostile before it proved anything

decision: re-baselined the replay probe and found the old baseline was a sample of one
why: HEAD showed a fatal failure in 2 of 3 passes, which looked like a regression from my director changes. a control at the pre-clue commit showed 1 of 3, so both arms sit at the same rate
evidence: control worktree at 9e1d921, 3 passes each arm
result: no regression. the 10 of 10 all-clean baseline everyone was comparing against was one lucky pass

decision: gave the replay probe a --repeat flag and made one pass report itself as a sample
why: a gate that fires a third of the time on known-good code is not a gate, it is a coin flip that teaches people to ignore it
result: baseline at --repeat 3 is 0/12 violence dropped, 0/6 fight-over-meta, 26/30 op defensible. a single pass immediately after 3 clean ones reported 1 FATAL, demonstrating the point

decision: no searching a room while a fight is on
why: the clue block appeared in every prompt including combat turns, which is implausible in the fiction and prompt noise exactly where getting the op right matters most
result: the rule reads w.mode not working.mode, so the turn a fight STARTS still carries the discovery the schema had offered. a mutant swapping the two is killed

decision: three reviewers with disjoint briefs (falsify claims, logic by probe, gaps and test quality) on three model families
why: a single shared brief makes reviewers converge; split briefs overlapped on one finding
result: 44 findings after dedup, 5 critical. every one triaged to fix, defer to a named unit, or narrow the claim

decision: adopted spec-kit with a constitution written from the invariants the code already keeps
why: the project is now spec-driven; a template constitution would have been aspirational
result: seven principles, and the tasks template no longer calls tests optional

decision: the mutation harness now scores a mutant only from its named test's own reporter event
why: any nonzero exit counted as a kill, so a poison mutant that broke an unrelated file and named a test that does not exist was certified covered
evidence: tools/mutate/json-reporter.mjs, poison lists reproduced on the old and new harness
result: old harness 2/2 poison KILLED, new harness 0/2 (STALE TEST NAME, ERRORED). real list 78/78, then 101/101 after the turn-loop fixes

decision: combat ends when nobody in the room is left to fight
why: combat checked for a hostile alive anywhere in the world, so the second foe of a delve kept the player pinned beside the first one's corpse, refused every exit
evidence: rules.ts finish() foeHere, mapgen.test.ts property test over 60 delves
result: 162 of 200 delves pinned before, 0 after

decision: built a playtest lever that plays whole sessions with the wandering DM and counts the endings
why: unit tests prove a rule on the turn they set up and cannot say whether a session can be finished, which is what the softlock got wrong while every test stayed green
evidence: tools/playtest/run.mjs --seeds 200, --app pointed at d3c1994 for the baseline
result: before: lantern 0 won 38 lost 162 timeout, delve 0 won 59 lost 137 stuck. after: lantern 22 won 28 lost 150 timeout, delve 74 won 97 lost 0 stuck. nothing pinned

decision: a session ends: won when every vow is kept, lost when the hero falls, and the engine takes no further turn
why: a fallen hero kept acting and a kept vow left the player in a room with a text box. both rated critical by review
evidence: outcomeOf() derived per call, SessionOver in takeTurn, 409 from the API, ending panel; drive.mjs delve seed 101 won on turn 20, tavern seed 1438 lost on turn 3
result: 107 of 107 mutants killed; the ending survives reload; a turn posted to a won session returns 409

decision: a title screen with continue, new tales and saves to resume or delete
why: the only way to start again was a URL parameter
evidence: DELETE /api/session/:id, list ordered by newest event row, drive.mjs recipe of nine asserts
result: created_at had one-second resolution and tied; ordering by event rowid fixed it. seven verify recipes rewritten and each rerun green

decision: the user widened finish-the-game to a D&D game on the 2024 rules, with campaigns as seasons and a separate forge
why: their answers: fuller 5e from the latest PHB, all twelve classes plus the Artificer and custom classes, death saves with a same-level replacement, three ability methods, a campaign generator whose contracts stay in sync with the game
evidence: specs/001-dnd-campaign-game/spec.md, twelve user stories, FR-001 to FR-020
result: scope is multi-session; the current engine was finished to a playable v1 first so there is a game while the redesign lands

decision: the rules base is SRD 5.2.1 under CC-BY-4.0, vendored as data with a build-time check against counts taken from the PDF
why: the 2024 Player's Handbook is not openly licensed; SRD 5.2.1 carries all twelve classes with one subclass each, 339 spells, 330 stat blocks and the 2024 encounter and XP tables. no dataset matches 5.2.1 exactly
result: the Artificer must be original expression; solo encounters built from the 2024 table run harder than their label

decision: a module is a graph of nodes joined by clues with pressure that moves on its own, and code owns every id, number and edge
why: the sources converge on the three-clue rule and its inversion, SRD encounter budgets, and a season arc threaded through self-contained modules; fixed difficulty curves and pillar ratios are folklore
result: a 3B model fills short local text under a schema; a validator and a human decide

decision: base the redesign on candidate A (the engine mints one list of offers for the UI, the DM and the rules), grafting B's combat turn budget and C's settlement funnel
why: three candidates on three model families; the cross-judge preferred B 28 to 27, the coordinator A 30 to 26. A deletes the refereeing surface every progress bug came from and falsifies its riskiest assumption first; the judge was right that A resolved a whole round per command
result: B's grid, per-save rules pinning and operation protocol rejected as cost without a requirement behind them

decision: two adversarial reviewers with split briefs attacked the synthesized plan before any code
why: a plan that eight phases build on is cheapest to fix on paper
result: the kill criterion now compares exact actions like for like and runs before the game changes; one model call per hero turn; hero-centric range bands; clock payoffs pulled into phase 1; decisions log their payload; persisted creation and fate phases

decision: one transaction helper in store.ts, so the rollback line exists once and its mutant is unambiguous again
